In the note below, bold, struck through, italic and a colour change happen inside a sentence rather than between sentences - which no run of separate text items can do. Look for straight right-hand edges on the two paragraphs above it, with the last line of each left short.

A table longer than a page, with one row taller than a page on its own. Look for the column headings repeating at the top of each page, and - the part worth checking - for the split row showing as many cells on the second page as the table has columns. A half-row with fewer cells is refused by a conformance checker and read aloud as nonsense. Under it, a table over a list with nothing in it: look for its headings staying, and one line across every column saying so. Then a note in mixed styles, taller than a page too: look for it carrying on overleaf with no line lost.

A contact sheet filled from the data: one picture is described in the template and repeated per record. Look for whole rows moving to the next page rather than a row of pictures being sliced, and for each picture keeping its proportions inside its cell.

Everything below this line comes from a second template file, spliced in before the layout ever ran. Look for it flowing on from this page rather than starting one of its own: a sub-template is part of the surrounding flow, and brings none of its own margins or page size.

Two barcodes, drawn by the engine rather than embedded as pictures, and both carrying values from the data. Look for the two titled below this one - numbered from it, so they read 5.1 and 5.2 without either number being typed anywhere - and for each carrying alternative text, without which a barcode is a figure with nothing to say.

Childs.Text: Fillable form fields: a tick box, two text boxes, a place to sign, and one more inside a table. Try typing in them - if they are flat, the document was rendered with the form flattened and the boxes are only a picture of somewhere to write. A signature is the case worth watching, because flattened it looks exactly the same and nothing on the page says so. The cell in the cost table is here because a field that is a table cell is tagged as a cell, not as a control, and its widget was reachable from nothing in the structure tree - which no reader shows you and only a validator refuses.

Childs.Text: {HeadingNumber}. A chart, and a picture with alpha

A chart drawn by another application as an SVG file and handed over in the data, so the template never changes. Zoom in: the curves stay sharp, because they are marks and not pixels. Select a label: it is text. The orange curve runs off its scale and stops at the top of the plot, which is a clip path. Under it, a PNG with an alpha channel: the band shows through its rings, which is a soft mask, and a checker wants to see one is allowed here.

Childs.AltText: Attendance over the year: visitors rise from 300 in January to 1,500 in July and fall back to 750 in December, while occupancy peaks above the scale in the summer.
The ACME mark, its rings transparent over a pale blue band

Childs.Text: {HeadingNumber}. What is here but not visible

Three things this file carries that no page can show you. A Factur-X invoice is attached - open the attachments pane to find factur-x.xml. The whole document is tagged, so a reader can announce headings, table cells and alternative text - the structure tree is where to check. And it claims PDF/A-3B and PDF/UA-1, which only a validator can confirm; a file that claims nothing is judged as PDF/A-1b instead, which forbids the transparency used by the watermark on every page.

The watermark behind this text is that transparency, drawn under the content rather than over it. The back of each sheet carries the terms, which is why the page count is higher than the sheet count printed in the footer.
